summary: This IEA report, CO2 Emissions in 2022, gives a complete picture of energy-related greenhouse gas emissions in 2022. It finds global CO2 emissions rose 0.9% (321 Mt) to a record 36.8 Gt, less than feared during the global energy crisis, because clean energy deployment and industrial curtailments offset much of the increase. The report breaks down growth by fuel (coal up, natural gas down, oil up), by sector (power up, industry down) and by region (China flat, EU down, US and Asia up), and is part of the IEA's support for the first global stocktake of the Paris Agreement.
one_line: IEA report finding global energy-related CO2 emissions hit a record 36.8 Gt in 2022, rising only 0.9% amid the energy crisis.
key_facts: Global energy-related CO2 emissions grew by 0.9% or 321 Mt in 2022, reaching a new all-time high of 36.8 Gt.
Emissions in 2021 rebounded by more than 6%, while emissions shrank by more than 5% in 2020 due to the Covid-19 pandemic.
Increased deployment of renewables, electric vehicles and heat pumps helped prevent an additional 550 Mt of CO2 emissions in 2022.
Extreme weather contributed 60 Mt of CO2 from heating and cooling demand, and nuclear power plants being offline added 55 Mt.
Global CO2 growth in 2022 was well below global GDP growth of 3.2%.
Emissions from natural gas fell by 1.6% or 118 Mt, with a 13.5% reduction in Europe.
Coal emissions grew by 1.6% or 243 Mt to a new all-time high of almost 15.5 Gt.
Oil emissions rose by 2.5% or 268 Mt to 11.2 Gt, with around half of the increase coming from aviation.
Electric car sales surpassed 10 million in 2022, exceeding 14% of global car sales.
Electricity and heat generation was the biggest sectoral increase, up 1.8% or 261 Mt, reaching 14.6 Gt.
Renewables met 90% of global growth in electricity demand, with solar PV and wind each increasing by around 275 TWh.
Industry emissions declined by 1.7% to 9.2 Gt, driven by a 161 Mt decrease in China's industry emissions.
China's emissions declined by 23 Mt or 0.2%, the first decline since structural reforms in 2015.
The European Union reduced CO2 emissions by 2.5% or 70 Mt, and wind and solar PV combined exceeded gas or nuclear generation for the first time.
US emissions grew by 0.8% or 36 Mt to 4.7 Gt, driven by an 89 Mt increase from natural gas.
Emissions from Asia's emerging market and developing economies, excluding China, grew 4.2% or 206 Mt.
